title: Research Bits: Sept. 8
gist: A three-item research digest covers an ultrathin amorphous-carbon dielectric for copper interconnects (with a planned TSMC reliability collaboration), a 600°C-capable silicon carbide complementary JFET from Kyoto University, and a KAIST/UNIST multilayer dielectric that stabilizes oxide vertical channel transistors for compute-in-memory — all incremental materials/device advances aimed at scaling interconnects and memory for the AI era.

themes.theme: Carbon insulating film for shrinking copper interconnects

insights.claim: Researchers from the National University of Singapore developed an atom-thin amorphous carbon film that maintains a low dielectric constant (k=1.35) across thicknesses from 0.8nm to 2.7nm, designed to insulate increasingly thin copper interconnect wires.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: A sub-nanometer ultralow-k insulator that also blocks copper diffusion could free up more physical space for the copper line itself, directly relevant to interconnect scaling roadmaps as node dimensions shrink further.
insights.quote: The film maintained a dielectric constant of 1.35 across thicknesses from 0.8nm to 2.7nm, withstanding strong electric fields while preventing copper ions from passing through it.

insights.claim: The film's insulating property comes from atomic disorder: the randomly arranged carbon atoms restrict how freely electrons respond to an electric field, allowing a low k-value to persist even at extreme thinness, despite carbon normally being a conductor.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: The disorder-driven insulation mechanism is a reusable materials-design principle for engineers seeking ultrathin dielectrics from otherwise-conductive elements as conventional low-k dielectrics run out of scaling headroom.
insights.quote: In our film, the atoms are arranged randomly. This disorder restricts how freely the electrons can respond to an electric field, allowing the k-value to remain low even when the film is extremely thin.

insights.claim: The film combines two functions in a single layer — low-k insulation and a copper diffusion barrier — by being grown via chemical vapor deposition below 300°C directly on silicon dioxide, copper, and cobalt, with uniform coverage across a four-inch wafer including sidewalls and corners of patterned structures, and it withstood electric fields of 28-31 megavolts per centimeter before losing insulating ability.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Merging the barrier and dielectric functions into one layer is a direct area-saving proposition for chipmakers fighting interconnect RC delay and shrinking metal pitch — a concrete efficiency lever for future process nodes.
insights.quote: The film gives us low-k insulation and a copper barrier in the same layer... combining these functions could free more space for the copper line itself.

insights.claim: The NUS team plans to collaborate directly with TSMC to test the carbon film's long-term reliability, scalability, and compatibility with existing fab processes.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: A named collaboration with the world's leading foundry signals this is being evaluated for near-term production relevance rather than staying purely academic — worth tracking for future TSMC process-node disclosures.
insights.quote: The team plans to collaborate with TSMC on testing long-term reliability, scalability, and compatibility with existing processes.

insights.claim: Kyoto University researchers developed silicon carbide complementary junction FETs (JFETs) that can operate at 600°C, arguing the field's prior lack of progress stemmed from applying silicon-era design thinking to a fundamentally different material rather than exploiting SiC's intrinsic properties.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: A 600°C-capable complementary JFET pushes power electronics into extreme-environment applications (aerospace, deep-well drilling, engine-adjacent automotive) beyond what silicon or standard SiC MOSFETs can survive.
insights.quote: We believe the lack of development is because the research community has been trying to apply silicon-era thinking to a fundamentally different material.

insights.claim: The new SiC JFET uses a bottom-gate design for better threshold-voltage controllability and well-based isolation instead of a semi-insulating substrate to suppress high-temperature leakage current, reducing leakage close to the theoretical limit for SiC.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Achieving near-theoretical-limit leakage at high temperature is a specific, measurable milestone that de-risks scaling this device toward wafer-level production for extreme-environment power electronics.
insights.quote: The combination reduced the leakage current to close to the theoretical limit for SiC.

insights.claim: Next steps for the Kyoto team are building more complex circuits, scaling to wafer-level production, and ensuring the whole package remains robust in extreme environments.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Still early-stage (device-level, not circuit- or wafer-level) — investors in SiC power players should treat this as a multi-year-out research lead rather than a near-term product input.
insights.quote: Next, the team plans to create more complex circuits, scaling up to wafer-level production, and ensuring the entire package remains robust in extreme environments.

insights.claim: KAIST and UNIST developed a multilayer SiN/SiO2/SiN interlayer dielectric that acts as an oxygen tunnel, stabilizing oxygen vacancy compensation in oxide vertical channel transistors (VCTs) while suppressing unwanted electrode oxidation, improving both current density and data retention.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Oxide VCTs are candidates for compute-in-memory devices; solving their long-standing instability problem via oxygen migration control is a prerequisite for commercializing 3D compute-in-memory at scale.
insights.quote: The silicon nitride/silicon dioxide/silicon nitride (SiN/SiO2/SiN) dielectric acts as an oxygen tunnel that enables stable compensation of oxygen vacancies in the oxide semiconductor while simultaneously suppressing unwanted oxidation at the electrode.

insights.claim: After more than ten million cycles of electrical stress testing, the threshold voltage shift of the new VCT structure remained below 50 millivolts, and the team successfully integrated the oxide semiconductor with conventional silicon CMOS technology.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Sub-50mV threshold drift after 10M+ cycles is a strong reliability data point that could accelerate commercialization timelines for oxide-based compute-in-memory relative to competing 3D memory approaches.
insights.quote: After more than ten million cycles of electrical stress testing, the threshold voltage shift remained below 50 millivolts.

insights.claim: The KAIST researcher framed this work's significance as addressing the long-standing instability problem in 3D devices through oxygen migration control, positioning it as key to commercializing ultra-low-power, high-performance compute-in-memory systems for the AI era.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Explicitly frames the research as AI-infrastructure-relevant (compute-in-memory to cut power for AI workloads), tying a materials-science result directly to the AI compute power bottleneck theme recurring across the industry.
insights.quote: We expect this technology to play a key role in accelerating the commercialization of ultra-low-power, high-performance compute-in-memory systems required for the AI era.
